sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: Change in the position of an object with respect to its surroundings over **time**.
An external push or pull that changes or tends to change the state of **rest** or **uniform motion** of a body.
Formulated by **Sir Isaac Newton** in his monumental work **Principia Mathematica** in **1687**.
High-yield general science topic frequently tested through numericals, definitions, and direct applications.
Based on the **SI system**: Force in **Newton (N)**, Acceleration in **m/s²**, Velocity in **m/s**.
Inertia, Linear Momentum, Conservation of Momentum, Friction, and Gravitational Force.
Crucial for scoring in the General Science section of UPSSSC PET across multiple shift papers.

items.title: Kinematics: Distance and Displacement
items.content:
• **Distance:** Total path length covered by a moving object; it is a **scalar quantity**.
• **Displacement:** Shortest straight-line distance between initial and final position; it is a **vector quantity**.
• Magnitude of displacement is **always less than or equal to** distance.
• **Mnemonic:** **SAD** (Scalar = Always Distance, Vector = Displacement) and **DV** (Displacement is Vector).

items.title: Speed and Velocity
items.content:
• **Speed:** Rate of change of distance with time; **scalar quantity**, SI unit **m/s**.
• **Velocity:** Rate of change of displacement with time; **vector quantity**, SI unit **m/s**.
• Uniform velocity requires both constant speed and constant **direction**.
• Average velocity equals total displacement divided by total time.

items.title: Acceleration and Equations of Motion
items.content:
• **Acceleration:** Rate of change of velocity with time ($a = \frac{v-u}{t}$); unit **m/s²**.
• Retardation is **negative acceleration** when velocity decreases.
• First Equation: **$v = u + at$**
• Second Equation: **$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$**
• Third Equation: **$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$**
• **Mnemonic for Equations:** **VUF** (Velocity = u + at), **SUT** (S = ut + half at square), **VUS** (v square = u square + 2as).

items.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
items.content:
• **First Law (Law of Inertia):** A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an **external force**.
• **Second Law (Law of Momentum):** Rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force ($F = ma$).
• **Third Law (Action-Reaction):** To every action, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**.
• **Mnemonic for Laws:** **FIN** (First = Inertia), **FMA** (Second = Force equals mass into acceleration), **AR** (Third = Action-Reaction).

items.title: Linear Momentum and Inertia
items.content:
• **Momentum ($p$):** Product of mass and velocity ($p = mv$); vector quantity, unit **kg·m/s**.
• **Inertia:** Inherent property of a body to resist changes in its state of **rest or motion**.
• Inertia is directly proportional to **mass** (heavier objects have more inertia).
• Inertia of rest, inertia of motion, and inertia of direction are the three main types.

items.definition: Remember scalar quantities with **'MDTSS'** (Mass, Distance, Time, Speed, Scalar) and remember that most vector quantities start with **'V'** (Velocity, Vector, Displacement, Acceleration, Force, Momentum).
Use **'IFM'** (I = Inertia / 1st Law, F = Force / 2nd Law, M = Momentum/Reaction / 3rd Law) to recall the core theme of each law in numerical order.

items.term: Trick 3: Equations of Motion Sign Convention
items.definition: For objects moving upwards against gravity, use **negative acceleration ($g$)**; for falling objects, use **positive acceleration ($g$)**. Remember: **'Up is negative, Down is positive'** for gravity in standard drop problems.

Dust falling when a carpet is beaten = **Inertia of Rest**. Passengers falling backward when a bus starts = **Inertia of Rest**. Passengers falling forward when brakes are applied = **Inertia of Motion**.

items.term: Trick 5: SI Unit Derivation for Force
items.definition: Remember **$F = ma$**. Mass is in **kg**, acceleration is in **m/s²**. Therefore, 1 Newton = **1 kg·m/s²**. Break down compound units to solve dimensional analysis questions easily.
Recoil of a gun, rocket propulsion, and bursting of firecrackers all work on the **Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum**. Remember: **'RRB'** (Recoil, Rocket, Bursting).

Students often treat distance and displacement as interchangeable. Remember that distance can **never be negative or zero** for a moving body, whereas displacement can be **zero** if a body returns to its starting point.

items.term: Mistake 2: Assuming Speed Equals Velocity Magnitude Always
items.definition: Speed and velocity magnitudes are equal only in **rectilinear motion in a single direction without turning**. If an object moves in a circle at constant speed, its velocity is **constantly changing** because direction changes.

Students think a force is required to keep an object moving uniformly. Correct fact: **No force is required** to maintain uniform motion in the absence of friction; force is only needed to change the state of motion.

items.term: Mistake 4: Action and Reaction on the Same Body
items.definition: Students mistakenly believe action and reaction cancel each other out. Correct fact: Action and reaction act on **two different bodies**, which is why motion is possible.
Writing acceleration unit as **m/s** instead of **m/s²**. m/s is for speed and velocity, while m/s² represents the rate of change of velocity per second.

Confusing real centripetal force with fictitious centrifugal force. Centripetal force acts **towards the center**, while centrifugal force is an apparent force experienced in a **rotating non-inertial frame**.
Motion is the continuous change in position of an object with respect to a **reference point** over time.
Scalar quantities have magnitude only (e.g., **speed, distance**), while vector quantities have both magnitude and direction (e.g., **velocity, displacement, force**).
Average speed = **Total Distance / Total Time**; Average Velocity = **Total Displacement / Total Time**.
Acceleration is the vector quantity representing the rate of change of velocity, measured in **m/s²**.
Valid only under **constant acceleration**: $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, and $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
Also known as the **Law of Inertia**, defining qualitative characteristics of force and inertial frames.
Provides the quantitative definition of force as the rate of change of momentum: **$F = ma$**.
States that forces always occur in pairs: **action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction**.
In the absence of an external force, the **total linear momentum** of a system remains constant.
Mass is the measure of inertia; **greater mass implies greater resistance** to acceleration.
Impulse equals the change in momentum: **$J = F \times \Delta t = \Delta p$**.
A contact force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact, categorized into **static, sliding, and rolling friction**.

upscNotes.content: For UPSSSC PET numerical questions, always convert all given values into **SI units** (meters, kilograms, seconds) before applying formulas like $F = ma$ or kinematic equations.
Memorize the exact definitions of scalar and vector quantities as UPSSSC frequently asks direct matching or multiple-choice questions from this list.
Be wary of questions asking about the net force on an object moving with constant velocity; students often assume force is non-zero, but by Newton's First Law, net force is **zero**.
Do not confuse the SI unit of momentum (**kg·m/s**) with the unit of force (**N** or **kg·m/s²**). Dimensional analysis questions often exploit this confusion.

keyTakeaways: Distance is scalar and path-dependent; displacement is vector and independent of path.
Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s².
Newton's First Law defines inertia; Second Law defines force ($F=ma$); Third Law defines action-reaction pairs.
Linear momentum ($p = mv$) is strictly conserved in isolated systems.
Equations of motion apply exclusively under conditions of constant acceleration.
Mass is the measure of inertia, meaning heavier objects resist changes in motion more strongly.
